- Oregon's first-in-the-nation experiment with decriminalizing drugs will expire on Sunday; a new law (HB4002) will recriminalize possession of small amounts of hard drugs.
- The law gives those caught with illicit drugs (fentanyl, heroin, meth) a choice: either be charged with possession or go to treatment (behavioral health program + deflection program) to avoid fines.
- Personal-use possession would be a misdemeanor punishable by up to six months in jail.
- It aims to make it easier for police to crack down on drug use in public and introduces harsher penalties for selling drugs near places like parks.
- The law encourages but does not mandate counties to create treatment alternatives to divert people from criminal justice toward addiction and mental health services.
- Supporters say this allows counties to develop programs based on resources; opponents say it may create a confusing and inequitable patchwork.
- Quote from Portland police chief Bob Day: criteria for deflection: no other charges, no warrants, no violent behavior, medically stable.
- If person meets deflection requirements, officers call county deflection dispatch line to provide info, determine eligibility, connect to mobile behavioral health outreach team that has 30 minutes to make contact.
- If behavioral health people cannot be there within 30 minutes, they go to jail; they can't wait.
